newsitem.title: TURKEY: FOCUS-Turkish shares slide on rating downgrade.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Turkish shares slide on rating downgrade.

text.p: Turkish shares slid four percent on Tuesday and the lira hovered near the psychologically important level of 100,000 to the dollar after the country's credit rating was downgraded by Japan's JCR agency.

The downgrading was not a major surprise to the share market but traders took the opportunity for profit-taking after an extended rally which has lifted the stock index over 100 percent since end-1995 -- a 25.4 percent rise in dollar terms.
"The JCR news sparked panic sales and sentiment turned from optimism to pessimism," said Acar Securities' Bulent Onder.
JCR downgraded from BB+ to BB its rating of Turkey's yen and Euroyen bond issues, which have so far totalled 115 billion yen ($103 million) in 1996.
The Istanbul stock exchange composite index closed 3.98 percent lower at 79.861.38 and off an intraday low of 79,131.77 after a day of heavy trading.

"They (JCR) had given enough hints about this and I didn't expect such a massive move by the market. It was just looking for an excuse for a sell-off," said Atilla Yesilada, director of research at leading Istanbul brokerage Global.
Analysts did not expect the downgrading to have any serious consequences and did not foresee near-term downgrades by other credit rating agencies.

"They made it clear they were not touching the rating until the IMF (International Monetary Fund) gives a signal," he said. Last month the IMF urged Turkey to make progress on a stability programme, seen as vital if a stand-by accord is to be granted.
"Clearly the international community is putting pressure on Turkey to act. If it doesn't, downgradings are going to come in like spring rain," Yesilada said.
The Islamist-led coalition of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has given the highest priority to accelerating the country's drifting privatisation plans to combat economic ills.

Two revenue-raising packages have already been announced by the four-month-old alliance to spearhead efforts to curb the yawning budget deficit. A third package expected to be unveiled soon is likely to include further privatisation plans.
Improving sell-offs are likely to keep shares on an upward course, analysts said. The government on Monday annnounced the sell-off of Etibank, which is being divided into three banks.
The credit rating downgrade also sparked some selling of the lira, which edged closer to the important psychological barrier of 100,000 to the dollar.
The lira eased to 99,600 against the dollar by the end of the day's trading, from 99,300 at the opening and 99,260 at Monday's close.
Yesilada said the central bank had the lira under control and was not going to allow it to weaken faster than monthly inflation, which at the consumer level stood at 6.5 percent in October.
A key question being asked is what the government intends to do with domestic debt since the Treasury has sharply curtailed domestic borrowing in the past two weeks, analysts said.
"If there is permanently less borrowing than there used to be this could send tremors through the currency market," said Yesilada.
The central bank continued heavy lira funding to relieve a persistent cash shortage, injecting 16.5 trillion lira via six-day repos at an average rate of 77.45 percent.
T-bill and bond yields firmed slightly after the statement from JCR, but later settled at lower levels. Yields slipped one percent ahead of the Treasury's 182-day bill auction set for Wednesday.
